one_liner: Bitdefender's x86/x64 instruction decoder in C with rich operand metadata; decode+format 1.4-1.8x Capstone's throughput in disas-bench.
what_it_does: A C11 x86/x64-only decoder with no allocation and no dependencies, also usable in kernel and hypervisor code. Two decode APIs exist. The legacy NdDecode/NdDecodeEx/NdDecodeWithContext calls fill a roughly 480-byte INSTRUX with every operand, explicit and implicit, plus access modes, flags access and CPUID feature data. The v3.0 NdDecodeMini call fills a 64-byte INSTRUX_MINI and returns operands and metadata on request (NdGetOperandMini, the bdx86_api_mini.h getters). NdToText or NdToTextMini formats Intel/MASM-style text. The repo also ships bdshemu, a small shellcode emulator, and Python and Rust bindings. The API differs from Capstone's, so switching means rewriting call sites.
how_it_is_fast: Decoding walks lookup tables generated offline by isagenerator from instruction-definition files: opcode map, then opcode byte, then ModRM.mod/reg/rm, mandatory prefix, mode and so on, until it reaches an instruction leaf (NdDecodeInstruction in bdx86_decoder.c). Nothing is allocated and there is no global state, so each call touches only the caller's INSTRUX. v3.0.0 moved validity checks into the tree walk so only instructions that need them pay for them. It also added the mini decoder, which skips operand and metadata expansion; disas-bench measured it at about 1.7x the legacy decoder for decode only (179 vs 104-106 MB/s). Options in ND_CONTEXT remove more work: ND_OPTION_ONLY_EXPLICIT_OPERANDS (the changelog claims 235 to 200 clocks per instruction), ND_OPTION_SKIP_ZERO_INSTRUX and ND_OPTION_SKIP_CACHE_IBYTES.
when_to_use: C or C++ tools that must decode and print large amounts of x86-64 code faster than Capstone: linear-sweep disassembly, binary scanners, malware triage.

Analysis that needs semantic detail per instruction (operand access modes, implicit operands such as RFLAGS and RSP, memory access, CPUID feature flag, valid modes) without a second pass; the legacy decoder provides it and still beat Capstone in decode+format.

Restricted environments such as Windows kernel drivers (MSBuild plus WDK targets), hypervisors and introspection agents, where the library must not allocate or depend on libc beyond nd_vsnprintf_s and nd_memset.
Decode-heavy work where only length, mnemonic and a few operands matter: NdDecodeMini with a 64-byte INSTRUX_MINI ran at about 179 MB/s decode only on both test CPUs.
Shellcode detection, using the bundled bdshemu emulator over the same decoder.
when_not_to_use: Maximum raw throughput when Rust or .NET is acceptable: in the same disas-bench charts, iced and yaxpeax-x86 decode+format run about 3.4-5.4x faster than bddisasm.
Non-x86 targets or multi-architecture tools: bddisasm decodes x86/x64 only, where Capstone covers ARM, MIPS, RISC-V and more.
AT&T syntax output: NdToText supports only Intel/MASM style.
Drop-in replacement of Capstone code: the API, instruction and register enums, and output text all differ.
Rust or Python users who want the v3 mini decoder: the published crate bddisasm 0.4.2 (2024-02-21) and PyPI pybddisasm 0.3.0 predate v3.0.0 (2025-07-14).

integration.dependencies: none. With the CMake build, bddisasm itself supplies nd_vsnprintf_s and nd_memset when libc has vsnprintf and memset. With the Make (Linux) and MSBuild (Windows) builds, the integrator must supply both functions.
integration.min_toolchain: C11 (C_STANDARD 11), CMake 3.16+; tested with GCC and Clang on Linux and MSVC (Visual Studio 2019) on Windows; the Windows kernel build needs MSBuild with WDK 1903. Python 3 is needed only to regenerate the decode tables.
integration.platforms: Decodes x86 and x86-64 code (16/32/64-bit modes). The library is portable C that runs in user, kernel and hypervisor mode on Windows and Linux per the README. The only measured host CPUs are x86-64 (Ryzen 9 9950X, i9-13900K, Core Ultra 7 165H).
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe by design per the README: no global mutable state and no allocation. Each thread passes its own INSTRUX/INSTRUX_MINI and ND_CONTEXT.

gotchas: The legacy NdDecodeEx zeroes the whole roughly 480-byte INSTRUX and decodes implicit operands on every call. disas-bench uses this default path; it does not pass ND_OPTION_ONLY_EXPLICIT_OPERANDS, and Capstone runs with detail off. The legacy decode+format row therefore compares full-detail bddisasm with no-detail Capstone, which understates bddisasm rather than inflating it. For throughput, use NdDecodeMini or the context options.

By default, decoding uses ND_VEND_ANY and ND_FEAT_ALL, so MPX, CET and CLDEMOTE encodings in the wide-NOP space decode as those instructions rather than as NOPs. Set FeatMode to ND_FEAT_NONE if you need NOP semantics; otherwise output can differ from other disassemblers.

Until 3.0.2 (commit 8017978, 2026-10-06), NdFetchModrmSibDisplacement decoded 16-bit displacement-only addressing wrongly: it skipped the displacement of mod=00 rm=110 and expected one for rm=101. The fix leaves the 32/64-bit path unchanged, so the 64-bit disas-bench numbers, measured on v3.0.0, are unaffected. Users decoding 16-bit code should take 3.0.2 or later.

The README speed figures (about 240 clocks per instruction legacy and 150 mini, on a Core Ultra 7 165H) have no baseline and do not say whether formatting is included. The disas-bench timings come from one clock() run per tool (20 passes over the 0x2460400-byte .text of a checked-in Firefox xul.dll) with no variance reported, and the chart values are bar lengths read off the PNGs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick bddisasm over Zydis (full decode+format about 33.3 MB/s against 46.8 for bddisasm on the 9950X chart, derived from page data) and Capstone when you need a C library with the richest per-instruction semantics and no allocation, kernel use included. Pick iced or yaxpeax-x86 when raw decode speed matters most and Rust or .NET bindings are fine. Pick diStorm3 or Intel XED when you need their particular C APIs or XED's Intel-authoritative tables.
verified_claims_summary: In athre0z/disas-bench, each harness does a linear sweep that decodes (and, for the format rows, prints) the 0x2460400-byte .text section of a Firefox xul.dll 20 times; harnesses are built with cc -O3. bddisasm v3.0.0 (CMake Release, LTO, NdDecodeEx plus NdToText) is compared with Capstone 5.0.6 (Makefile -O3, x86 only, cs_disasm_iter with detail off). Decode+format: 46.8 vs 27.5 MB/s on a Ryzen 9 9950X with GCC 13.3, and 35.6 vs 25.9 MB/s on an i9-13900K with GCC 14.2 (1.70x and 1.37x); the mini decoder reaches 1.77x and 1.51x (ratios derived from chart readings).
status_note: Actively maintained by Bitdefender: v3.0.3 released 2026-10-07 after a 16-bit addressing fix on 2026-10-06. Apache-2.0, plain C11 with no dependencies, available through vcpkg and CMake FetchContent, so it is easy to vendor.
